overview: Andronovo groups related Bronze Age traditions, including Alakul and Fedorovo, across Central Asia. These were varied communities, not one empire. The map's 2000-1500 BCE interval and continuous outline simplify unevenly documented distributions; some evidence below is later.

periods.title: Early second-millennium connections
periods.summary: Sintashta and Petrovka settlements form important neighboring and preceding contexts; Andronovo classification and chronology vary regionally.

periods.title: Regional communities and craft networks
periods.summary: Dated cemeteries at Lisakovsk and settlements farther east reveal overlapping local traditions. The map ends before the full archaeological sequence does.

sections.title: A connected landscape, investigated site by site

items.text: Andronovo's importance lies in networks of herding communities and craftspeople across the steppe and mountain margins. Bronze objects and raw materials moved between regions, while pottery-making could remain distinctly local. The resulting connections carried techniques and materials over great distances without requiring a single capital or central government.

Afanasevo belongs to an earlier regional Bronze Age background. Sintashta, with its fortified settlements and chariot burials, has its own archaeological identity and its own atlas record. Andronovo includes later and overlapping traditions whose relationship to these neighbors must be examined through dated sites, rather than merging every steppe label into one civilization.

Wood can change a timeline. At Lisakovsk on the upper Tobol, researchers matched tree rings and radiocarbon measurements from burial timbers. Their adjusted results placed three studied cemeteries roughly between 1780 and 1660 BCE, earlier than older estimates based on pottery alone. The timber supplied a check on the ceramic calendar.

Bronze Age finds from Atasu, Myrzhik and other Kazakh sites reveal mining, smelting and metalworking centers. The National Museum displays this evidence alongside jewelry and ceramics. Producing an ornament or tool required a whole chain of work: obtaining ore, extracting metal and shaping the finished object. The wider Bronze Age material should not all be squeezed into this map's five centuries.

At Adunqiaolu in northwestern Xinjiang, excavators uncovered substantial stone-founded buildings. House F1 had internal divisions and probable storage pits; buildings F2 and F3 were added beside it. These structures provide evidence of repeated investment in a place to live and work. They do not tell us exactly how many relatives shared dinner or whether every room belonged to one family.

Was Adunqiaolu a winter home? Researchers compared its sheltered location with modern seasonal camps, then examined pollen and plant particles in ancient sheep dung. Those remains support autumn or winter use. Keeping animals fed through snow season demanded detailed knowledge of pastures and shelter. Modern herders help researchers test the idea; their customs are not automatically Bronze Age customs.

The Adunqiaolu house sequence continued into the later second millennium BCE, beyond this map's endpoint. Charred barley from its deposits was directly dated from the late seventeenth to thirteenth centuries BCE; millet was also found but not separately dated. The small grain assemblage and lack of crop-processing debris suggest food arriving from cultivation elsewhere, rather than fields beside this high winter camp.

Sheep dung may have done a second job after leaving the sheep: fuel. At Adunqiaolu, burned weed seeds and preserved dung cluster in a domestic area, supporting storage and burning of dung. Other seed concentrations may mark stored animal fodder. This is evidence about heating and household organization; the excavations cited here do not establish a toilet system.

A dental study examined 1,173 teeth from 77 people at Bestamak and Lisakovsk combined. Both groups showed patterns consistent with protein-rich diets that produced relatively little tooth decay, although calculus, abscesses and gum-related damage still occurred. Lisakovsk's teeth reveal a somewhat healthier later population, not a pain-free world or proof of a particular remedy.

At Lisakovsk, adult males and females had no significant differences in the dental conditions examined, even though their burial treatment differed. That combination is a useful reminder that grave goods and everyday experience can tell different stories. Older people generally showed more gum-related disease than younger people. Teeth offer a glimpse of lives that elaborate objects alone cannot supply.

sections.title: Making things, remembering people and the missing words

items.text: Old cloth could become a potter's tool. Research on Bronze Age steppe ceramics found fabric impressions inside vessels, left when cloth helped shape or support wet clay; some cloths were reused. At Begash, one published plain-weave impression belongs to a broad 1650-1000 BCE phase. It preserves a trace of fabric even after the cloth itself has vanished, with part of that evidence later than this map.

Why do some pots look almost woven? A 2018 experimental study recreated geometric designs using tablet weaving and compared them with Andronovo pottery decoration. The results support the possibility that textile patterns inspired pot designs. This remains an interpretation tested by making things, not a discovery that every patterned pot was a coded message.

Pottery also records learning. Clay preparation and vessel building involved repeated instruction and practice, with considerable local variation. Similar-looking jars could result from different hand movements. Researchers can investigate these skills without inventing classrooms or assuming all potters were women.

Lisakovsk's burial structures included floor planks, beams, cover poles and wooden wall supports. Pine supplied the samples used for tree-ring dating, while birch was also present. Preparing these graves required woodworking and shared labor as well as remembrance. The surviving construction shows what people made for the dead; it does not preserve their spoken funeral prayers.

No securely attested Andronovo written sentence is available in the evidence used here. Scholars commonly connect these traditions with Indo-Iranian languages and study later languages for possible ancient loans, but those comparisons do not supply an original inscription. Pottery decoration is not a verified alphabet. A reconstructed phrase would therefore give a false impression of a surviving Bronze Age voice.

ending.text: The map cutoff at 1500 BCE is not a documented collapse. Regional traditions continued changing through the later second millennium BCE. Their transformations do not mark the defeat of one kingdom or the disappearance of its inhabitants.
